title: CoachGPT: A Scaffolding-based Academic Writing Assistant
venue: Proceedings of the 48th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR '25)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a key concern with large language models in education: while tools such as ChatGPT can generate text fluently, they may undermine learning by producing essays for students instead of teaching them how to write. The authors focus on academic writing support, especially for novice writers and second-language writers who may lack access to instructors or other educational resources. The paper asks how an LLM-based writing assistant can be designed to provide instructional scaffolding rather than simply generating finished text.

To address this problem, the authors developed CoachGPT, a web-based academic writing assistant built around an 11-stage scaffolding structure. The system guides users through pre-writing, identifying resources, forming a thesis statement, building an outline, drafting introduction/body/conclusion paragraphs, revising, evaluating word choice, and checking grammar. Prompt engineering techniques were used to keep the model in a coaching role, including persona prompting, constraints against rewriting student work, criteria-based feedback, structured output, and input validation. The system was implemented as an online application using a Vue/Nuxt frontend, FastAPI and LangChain backend, and MySQL database.

The empirical component is a small qualitative user study using cognitive interviews with three users identified by pseudonyms: two with some academic writing experience and one with minimal experience. The paper does not provide explicit institutional enrollment status for participants, but the context is academic writing support for students, and the work is situated at the University of Delaware in the United States. The study examined user experience with personalization, interface navigation, and the usefulness of the scaffolding structure.

The main conclusion is that CoachGPT appears useful as a responsible academic writing assistant that offers attentive, adaptive feedback and a user-friendly interface. Participants reported that the personalized feedback made them feel heard and supported, and they valued the scaffolded guidance. At the same time, the study revealed areas for improvement, including simplifying terminology in early stages, improving thesis and counterargument support, and making grammar feedback more specific. Overall, the paper presents CoachGPT as a promising educationally oriented alternative to general-purpose text generation tools, though the evidence is preliminary and based on a very small qualitative study.

identified_tools.name: CoachGPT
identified_tools.description: An LLM-based academic writing assistant web application that uses a scaffolding workflow to guide writers through stages such as pre-writing, thesis development, outlining, paragraph drafting, revising, word choice evaluation, and grammar checking, while providing personalized feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a scaffolding-based academic writing assistant for novice and developing academic writers, including second-language writers, with qualitative user testing focused on usefulness, personalized feedback, interface/navigation, and support across writing stages.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative user study with three participants (Alex, Taylor, and Jamie; n=3), users reported that CoachGPT was useful for academic writing and provided personalized, attentive, and adaptive feedback during revision. The paper states that the user study 'proves the effectiveness' of CoachGPT, but reports no quantitative learning outcome measures or effect sizes.
findings.measure: Qualitative user perceptions of usefulness and personalized writing support in academic writing

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that CoachGPT had an intuitive, user-friendly interface and easy navigation, though they suggested improvements such as being able to view or hide the outline while writing. These findings are based on qualitative cognitive interviews only, with no quantitative usability metrics reported.
findings.measure: Qualitative user experience with navigation and interface usability

findings.finding_summary: Users valued CoachGPT's scaffolding and grammar feedback, but also identified shortcomings: Jamie found the term 'key questions' confusing, all users wanted more formulaic thesis templates, Alex noted issues with counterargument detection, and grammar feedback lacked specific in-text error highlighting compared with Grammarly. This indicates perceived usefulness alongside notable design and feedback limitations.
findings.measure: Qualitative perceptions of scaffolding clarity and writing-feedback quality

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical paper with a user study, but the evidence is based on qualitative cognitive interviews with only three participants and no controlled comparison, validated outcome measure, or quantitative effect estimate.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported impacts are positive but based on small-sample qualitative perceptions rather than measurable gains in writing performance, so the magnitude of impact is unclear.
